newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Right ponders new party to steal FN votes.
newsitem.headline: French Right ponders new party to steal FN votes.

text.p: An aide to French former interior minister Charles Pasqua raised the possibility on Tuesday of forming a political party to the right of the neo-Gaullist RPR to capture votes from the far-right National Front.

The French daily Le Monde quoted William Abitbol as saying the anti-imigrant Front's "expected but stupefying" victory on Sunday in municipal elections in the southern town of Vitrolles was "a victory for democracy but a defeat for the Republic."

Le Monde said Abitbol and other political allies of Pasqua were considering creating a political movement based on the nationalist ideas of the late General Charles de Gaulle, but free of the Front's xenophobia.

"The only reference that people relate to is their country, their motherland," Abitbol was quoted as saying. "If no one else can bring those answers the National Front is inevitably going to gain power."

In a vote that shocked the political establishment, Catherine Megret, wife of the Front's number two, captured the Vitrolles city hall from Socialist Jean-Jacques Anglade by 52.5 to 42.5 percent of the votes.

Clashes broke out overnight in the depressed town, with anti-Front youths attacking a school and shattering windscreens of parked cars. Police detained 10 protesters, four of whom were later released.

A court in nearby Aix-en-Provence on Tuesday jailed a youth for four months for throwing stones at police. A Front supporter was given a two-month suspended sentence and another was fined in connection with campaign incidents.

Abitbol did not say if a new party could be launched in time to contest the next general election, due in March 1998. Pasqua, as a hardline interior minister, pushed through tough restrictions to immigration laws in a bid to pull the rug from under the anti-immigrant National Front.
The ruling centre-right is uncertain how to contain the rise of the National Front.

The candidate of the ruling coalition pulled out from the run-off in Vitrolles after coming third in the first round, but the Socialists blamed Megret's win on the failure of mainstream conservatives to back the "anti-fascist" candidate in sufficient numbers.
Vitrolles is the fourth municipality to fall into the hands of the Front after its candidates claimed Toulon, Orange and Marignane in 1995 municipal elections.

Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, who advocates sending home France's three million mostly North African immigrants and reserving jobs, housing and welfare benefits for French nationals, won 15 percent of the vote in 1995 presidential elections.
